Google alters its cloud playbook, enlisting partners to sell more AI chips
headlines.summary: Google is opening its TPU business beyond its own cloud as custom chips become a bigger engine for growth.
headlines.article_text: Google alters cloud playbook turning to partners to sell more AI chips Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Google started working on in-house silicon in 2013, but didn't begin selling its tensor processing units to outside customers until the second quarter of this year. Now the company is tapping Oracle's cloud as another avenue for selling TPUs as it tries to bolster competition with Nvidia in the AI chip market. Thomas Kurian, Google's cloud boss, spent more than 20 years at Oracle before joining Google in 2018. In this article GOOGL ORCL Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT Thomas Kurian, chief executive officer of cloud services at Google LLC, speaks during the Google Cloud Next event in San Francisco on April 9, 2019. Michael Short | Bloomberg | Getty Images Google has spent years pitching customers on the advantage of buying its chips, models and cloud services in one place, offering a full stack that rivals Amazon and Microsoft have tried to replicate. Now, the company is pushing its equipment outside of its own walls to reach more customers and build a bigger business around artificial intelligence chips, a market that Nvidia has dominated. A day ahead of its third-quarter earnings report, Alphabet said Tuesday that Oracle will offer Google's tensor processing units, or TPUs, the custom chips the internet giant has been developing since 2013 . It's the first time customers will be able to access TPUs outside of Google's infrastructure, and shows that cloud boss Thomas Kurian, who previously spent more than 20 years at Oracle, is looking elsewhere for growth. "They're a very strong competitor, and it's very possible that they could eventually take market share from Nvidia," said Chris Ballard, managing director of Check Capital Management, referring to Google's position in chips. Kurian, who joined Google in late 2018, is operating from a position of strength. Analysts expect Google Cloud revenue to jump about 90% from a year earlier, after growing 82% in the second quarter , with TPUs contributing to its momentum. watch now VIDEO 3:06 03:06 Google's AI spend under scrutiny: Here's what to know Squawk Box "Google was great at doing its own thing, but it was never able to serve customers," said Uday Cheruvu, a portfolio manager at Harding Loevner, which owns Alphabet shares. "That mindset has changed." Google opened up TPUs to outside data centers in the second quarter, before this week's announcement with Oracle. Estimates for the TPU business vary widely, but they all point to significant growth. TD Cowen models $9.4 billion in TPU sales for the second half of this year and $62.5 billion for 2027. Wells Fargo expects about $9 billion in third-quarter sales and $99 billion next year. CFO Anat Ashkenazi said on the last earnings call in July that only a small portion of TPU revenue from existing agreements will be recognized this year, with the "vast majority" coming in 2027. She also said Google planned to use more outside capacity in the third quarter while the company builds out its own infrastructure. With $25 billion in second-quarter cloud revenue, Google trailed Amazon Web Services at $42 billion and Microsoft Azure at $29 billion. But Google is growing the fastest. "It's almost like the bigger the pie is getting, the faster they're accelerating into it," said Ballard, whose firm owned about $236 million in Alphabet stock as of June 30. watch now VIDEO 1:14 01:14 Wall Street expects Google Cloud growth to top 90% as Search slows Closing Bell 'Optimize the whole stack' While Kurian aims to get more TPUs into the market by turning to outside partners, he has to balance the benefits of building the customer base with his company's own technology needs. At a Goldman Sachs conference in September, Kurian said Google's AI servers pay for themselves in under two years, and servers running its own silicon reach payback in roughly half that time. "It's because we can optimize that whole stack," Kurian said. Industry research SemiAnalysis estimates that Google's latest Ironwood TPU costs about 44% less to own and operate than an Nvidia GB200 server. There's also the margin hit that comes with external TPU sales. TD Cowen estimates a 20% operating margin on TPU sales, compared with an overall cloud margin of about 35% last quarter. Cheruvu said he doesn't think Google's cloud operating margin could widen much beyond the mid-30s. Google declined comment. watch now VIDEO 1:36 01:36 Why Anthropic’s IPO is risky business Tech Google's biggest TPU customer is one of its top AI competitors. Anthropic, whose Claude models compete with Gemini, agreed last October to use up to 1 million TPUs in a deal worth tens of billions of dollars. Mizuho says that agreement brings nearly a gigawatt of capacity online this year and describes the relationship as Google "arming its closest model competitor." OpenAI is also planning to buy TPUs from Google, CNBC confirmed after The Information first reported on the ChatGPT maker's intentions on Tuesday. Anthropic is getting outside help to finance its Google silicon. This week, Broadcom , which works with Google on TPUs, detailed a $63 billion vehicle backed by Blackstone and three big banks that will buy TPUs and networking gear from Broadcom and lease them to Anthropic for five years. According to analysts from William Blair, the financing plan covers about half of Anthropic's 2027 needs, which suggests more financing is coming. In its initial public offering filing on Monday, Anthropic said it uses silicon from Google, Amazon, Nvidia and Advanced Micro Devices , allowing the company to "select chips based on the best price-performance and efficiency characteristics for each workload." Regarding Google and Broadcom, Anthropic said the partnerships "provide us with access to compute capacity powered by Google TPUs across multiple generations of the TPU platform." headlines.article_text: CNBC Technology Summit 2026: AI news and live updates Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu CNBC's Jon Fortt interviews Wikipedia Founder Jimmy Wales at the 2025 CNBC Technology Executive Council Summit in New York on October 28, 2025 CNBC At a defining moment for business and technology, artificial intelligence is transforming how organizations operate — and introducing new complexities for the leaders responsible for what comes next. So how are companies adapting and shaping technology's next era — from compute ROI and cybersecurity to regulation and quantum computing? CNBC is convening technology executives, industry experts, and CNBC journalists at the annual Technology Executive Council Summit in New York today to discuss the increasingly central role that technology leaders are playing in this transformation. The TEC Summit is an exclusive event for members; learn more about the TEC and apply for membership at www.cnbccouncils.com/tec . 25 Min Ago The tech-focused discussions at the CNBC WEC Summit CNBC Workforce Executive Council members speak with CNBC's Sharon Epperson at the 2026 CNBC Workforce Executive Council Summit in New York City on October 27, 2026. CNBC Yesterday, CNBC's Workforce Executive Council held its annual Summit , and the discussion of how human resources professionals help workers adapt to this new AI age was at the top of the agenda. Walmart , the biggest private employer in the world, asked its 2.1 million associates in June that exact question for the first time, trying to get a sense of how one of the most diverse workforces is experiencing AI. What it found, based on more than 1.7 million survey responses, is that while workers have different levels of familiarity and comfort with AI, training and experience with the technology matters. Seventy-seven percent of Walmart's office-based associates said are excited about AI's potential to improve their work, Walmart Chief People Officer for Associate Experience and Digital Maren Waggoner told CNBC's Leslie Picker at the WEC Summit. And as for Walmart's U.S. frontline associates, 84% said they are confident using digital tools, a reflection of the AI-powered tools that many of them are now using in their roles, she said. "We've given them certificates, we've given them training programs and tools, and so they're using it in their day-to-day," Waggoner said. Jill Bruning, chief technology officer of Amentum and a member of the CNBC Technology Executive Council, said at the WEC Summit that strategy should be evolved to be humans in the lead. "There's an AI curve, and we see it. It's going up and it's going fast and has a lot of attributes to it; it's quicker than anything we've seen before," Bruning told CNBC's Susan Caminiti. "So when you think about people on that curve … that gap is getting bigger every day." Bruning said she doesn't know if leadership is adapting fast enough to the technology, and that is creating additional challenges with upskilling as well as what tasks are being delegated to AI. "So your delegation skills are different, and then how do we tell the agents what to do? How do we define that role? She said. "That's human over the loop, not in the loop. We're still in charge." For more from the CNBC WEC Summit, you can see the full live blog here . — Ian Thomas 42 Min Ago Today's top tech headlines A drone view shows a data center at the Google Storey County Campus in the Tahoe-Reno Industrial Center in Sparks, Nevada, Oct. 9, 2026. Daniel Cole | Reuters Here are some of the top tech-focused headlines from CNBC this morning: Google alters its cloud playbook, enlisting partners to sell more AI chips . Google started working on in-house silicon in 2013, but didn't begin selling its tensor processing units (TPUs) to outside customers until the second quarter of this year. Now the company is tapping Oracle's cloud as another avenue for selling TPUs as it tries to bolster competition with Nvidia in the AI chip market. Anthropic’s cash pile towers over nearly every U.S. company . Anthropic had $112.4 billion in cash and cash equivalents and $19.3 billion in short-term investments as of June 30. That exceeded every non-bank U.S. company in CNBC and S&P Capital IQ data except Berkshire Hathaway and Alphabet. Amazon’s anti-tokenmaxxing memo says engineers should be pickier about using AI . Amazon discouraged teams from relying solely on token usage or code generation as measurements of AI adoption, calling them "deeply flawed" metrics in an internal memo. The memo revises how the company defines the role of software development engineers and managers in the age of AI. — Ian Thomas 51 Min Ago What's on the agenda at this year's TEC Summit Cheng Xin | Getty Images This year's TEC Summit is focusing on what is coming next in AI, whether that's how companies are adapting their strategies based on the advancement in the technology to how they're controlling the costs related to that build out. Discussions will also center on AI regulation, agents, how workers are using the technology and where this acceleration of AI is taking society. Speakers include: Campbell Brown, Forum AI Founder & CEO : Brown will be discussing AI regulation, independent evaluation, what that looks like and how companies can use AI that can be trusted. Nigel Vaz, Publicis Sapient CEO : Vaz is at the center of how companies are rethinking their business models amid the AI age, and why that's harder than learning how to use the technology itself. Calix CEO Michael Weening and CPO Shane Eleniak : Members of the team at Calix will pull back the curtain on how strategic AI decisions are made and implemented across the organization. Keia Cole, Brooklyn Sports & Entertainment Chief Digital Officer : Technology is also transforming the sports industry, and Cole will discuss how AI is being used at the Barclays Center and within the Brooklyn Nets and New York Liberty teams to make sports fans more connected and in touch. Jason Gowans, Levi Strauss Chief Digital & Technology Officer : Organizations are aiming to empower workers and customers with AI tools. Gowans will be sharing his approach to embedding AI into the everyday shopping experience. Jeetu Patel, Cisco President & Chief Product Officer : Rogue AI agents show no signs of slowing down, but Patel said companies need to think about them like they are teenagers. He'll discuss ways companies can safely harness the power of agents and what it means to parent them. — Ian Thomas How de-extincting dire wolves and woolly mammoths may extend human life Colleen McKown America's AI backlash: How the effort to keep worker trust is evolving inside companies Rachel Curry watch now watch now VIDEO 01:45 CNBC TEC Survey: Respondents say AI is accelerating cyber risk faster than organizations can adapt Seema Mody Read More
